title: Mutations in CYP24A1 and idiopathic infantile hypercalcemia
authors: Schlingmann KP, Kaufmann M, Weber S, Irwin A, Goos C, John U, et al.
population: Familial cases of idiopathic infantile hypercalcaemia with suspected autosomal recessive inheritance, and a second cohort of infants with severe hypercalcaemia after bolus vitamin D prophylaxis
funder: not stated in the abstract; the full text was not accessible (HTTP 403 at nejm.org), so the funding statement was not read.
result: Abstract: idiopathic infantile hypercalcaemia is characterised by severe hypercalcaemia, failure to thrive, vomiting, dehydration and nephrocalcinosis; its incidence rose in Britain in the 1950s during a period of high vitamin D supplementation in fortified milk. Recessive mutations in CYP24A1, encoding the 24-hydroxylase that degrades 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3, were found in six affected children and in a second cohort of infants in whom severe hypercalcaemia developed after bolus prophylaxis with vitamin D; all mutations caused complete loss of function. CYP24A1 mutations are a genetic risk factor for symptomatic hypercalcaemia that may be triggered by vitamin D prophylaxis in otherwise apparently healthy infants.
